sections.title: The Severity of the Prohibition of Idolatry
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to believe in God, that He is the sole Creator of the world and He guides it, and it is forbidden to believe that there is any other deity besides Him, as it is stated (Shemot 20:2-3): "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before Me." This prohibition is called "avoda zara" (idolatry, literally "foreign worship"), and its meaning is that instead of believing that God is the Creator and Sustainer of the world and the Master of all forces, and that only He is fit to be worshipped, a person believes that foreign forces besides Him have independent power, and he worships them in order to derive benefit from them.

Idolatry in partnership (shituf) is also forbidden. That is, even one who knows that God is the God of gods, if he believes that alongside Him or beneath Him there is an additional power that has the choice to decide how to act, and therefore he worships it as well in order to receive help from it, he is worshipping idolatry in partnership, and his law is that of one who worships idolatry. As it is stated (Shemot 20:3): "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 1:6; Yere'im 243; Semag, negative commandment 1; below, section 4).

The Sages said (Sifrei, Re'eh 54): "Whoever acknowledges idolatry denies the entire Torah, and whoever denies idolatry acknowledges the entire Torah." We also learn this from what is stated (Bamidbar 15:22-23): "And if you err and do not observe all these commandments which the Lord spoke to Moshe, all that the Lord commanded you by the hand of Moshe, from the day that the Lord commanded and onward throughout your generations." The Sages explained that this refers to the mitzva that is equal to all the mitzvot, namely idolatry, and it is the mitzva "which the Lord commanded you," since the first two mitzvot of the Ten Commandments, "'I am' and 'You shall have no' – we heard them from the mouth of the Almighty" (Horayot 8a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 2:4).

The Sages said (Kiddushin 39b) that the prohibition of idolatry is more severe than all other sins, for with all other sins, a person who thought an evil thought and did not come to act on it is not punished for his thought. Whereas with idolatry, one is punished even for an evil thought, as it is stated (Yeḥezkel 14:5): "That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from Me through their idols."

Because of the great severity of the prohibition of idolatry, a Jew is commanded to give up his life rather than desecrate God's name through idolatry, as it is stated (Devarim 6:4-5): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might." "'With all your soul' – even if He takes your soul" (Mishna Berakhot 9:5). It is likewise stated (Vayikra 22:32): "You shall not desecrate My holy name, and I will be sanctified among the children of Israel; I am the Lord who sanctifies you." The laws of self-sacrifice (mesirut nefesh) will be explained at length below in chapter 4.

One who worships idolatry intentionally before witnesses, after they warned him and cautioned him not to worship idolatry, is liable to death by stoning. As it is stated (Devarim 17:2-7): "If there is found among you, within any of your gates which the Lord your God gives you, a man or a woman who does what is evil in the eyes of the Lord your God, in transgressing His covenant, and has gone and worshipped other gods and bowed down to them, or to the sun or to the moon or to any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded; and it is told to you, and you hear of it, then you shall inquire diligently, and behold, if it is true and the thing certain, that this abomination has been done in Israel, then you shall bring forth that man or that woman who has done this evil thing to your gates, the man or the woman, and you shall stone them with stones, and they shall die. By the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses shall he who is to die be put to death; he shall not be put to death by the mouth of one witness. The hand of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people; and you shall eradicate the evil from your midst."

sections.title: Punishments in Practice, and Deterrence
sections.html:
For the gravest sins, most of which concern idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed, the Torah set the punishment of death. There are four kinds of death penalty in the Torah – stoning, burning, the sword and strangulation – and the most severe of them is stoning, which is the penalty incurred by one who worships idolatry. To strengthen the deterrence against those who sin through idolatry, the Torah commanded that the idol worshipper be put to death at the gate of the city in which he sinned. In addition, since his sin involved public rebellion against God, after his execution it is a mitzva to hang him on a wooden beam. However, he is not left hanging for long, because man was created in the image of God, and when his hanging is prolonged, the honour of Heaven is desecrated (Sanhedrin 46a-b). Therefore, he is hung shortly before sunset, and at sunset he is taken down from the hanging. As it is stated (Devarim 21:22-23): "And if a man has committed a sin deserving death, and he is put to death, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but you shall surely bury him that day, for a hanged man is a curse of God; and you shall not defile your land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance" (Sanhedrin 45b; Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 15:2, 6). For only one other transgression did the Torah set the punishment of stoning and hanging, namely the blasphemer, for that too involves public rebellion against God (below, section 8).

The authority to impose a death sentence is given to a Minor Sanhedrin, which consists of twenty-three ordained judges. And although there are thirty-six transgressions in the Torah whose punishment is death at the hands of the court (Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 15:10-13), in practice, very few sinners were executed. The Sages said of a Sanhedrin that executed one person in seven years that it is called "destructive," and some say one in seventy years (Mishna Makkot 1:10). This is because the courts were diligent about two principles simultaneously. On the one hand, when a person sinned publicly and intentionally and was found guilty, they punished him with death as the Torah commands, and thus sinners were afraid to sin publicly. On the other hand, they were extremely careful about passing judgment, and for every slight doubt they exempted the sinner from the death penalty. For example, if it was not certain that the sinner knew at the time he sinned that his act was forbidden and that its punishment was death, they would not execute him. Therefore, only if they warned him close to the act of the sin, and it was absolutely clear that the sinner heard their warning and understood that if he sinned he would be put to death by the court, and he sinned nonetheless, is he liable to death. In practice, there is hardly anyone who would sin after such a warning. Therefore, most of those executed were murderers who, out of great anger, could not control their impulses, and murdered despite the warning. The result was that, in practice, far fewer people were executed among the people of Israel than was customary in other kingdoms and pagan religions.

In addition, the Great Court (the Great Sanhedrin) has the authority to abolish the death penalty in Israel, as they did at the end of the Second Temple period. In those days the Sages saw that murderers had multiplied and the death penalty no longer deterred, and if they carried out the death penalties, they would have to execute too many people without their execution helping to prevent further murders. To avoid this, they went into exile from their place in the Chamber of Hewn Stone (Lishkat Ha-gazit) adjacent to the Temple to a nearby street, and thereby lost the authority to execute a person, for only when the Great Court sits adjacent to the Temple do the courts have the authority to put a person to death (Avoda Zara 8b, Rabbeinu Ḥananel).

And although in practice the court would execute people for their sins only in very rare cases, and in addition, many generations have passed since the court went into exile from the Chamber of Hewn Stone adjacent to the Temple and thereby lost its authority to execute sinners, in the course of study it is customary to call all those who intentionally commit one of the grave sins whose punishment is death "ḥayavei mita" (those liable to death). There are three reasons for this: 1) To express the severity of the sins, for in principle this is the punishment they deserve. 2) In very rare cases this was indeed their punishment. 3) Those who commit the grave sins are indeed liable to death at the hands of Heaven through karet. For anyone who intentionally commits a transgression for which, under certain conditions, one is liable to death by the court, is punished at the hands of Heaven with karet, that is, death through the shortening of one's days (Mo'ed Katan 28a). However, those liable to karet who repented are forgiven their sin and are exempt from the punishment of karet (Razah and Ramban).1

sections.title: The Prohibitions of Idolatry
sections.html:
One who intentionally worships one of the idols according to the rite that its worshippers established for it is liable to death. Even when the rite established for that idol appears degrading, such as Ba'al Pe'or, which was worshipped by relieving oneself before it, or Markulis (Mercury), which was worshipped by throwing stones at it – one who does this intentionally is liable to death.

In addition, one who worships an idol with one of the four important services that were performed in the Temple, even if the worshippers of that idol are not accustomed to worship it in that way, is liable to death. These are the four services: 1) Prostration. 2) Zevi'ḥa – slaughtering a sacrifice. 3) Haktara – burning a sacrifice on the altar. 4) Nisukh – pouring wine or sprinkling blood in honour of the idol (Sanhedrin 60b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:2-3).

Likewise, one who accepts an idol upon himself, even though he did not perform any act, since through speech he accepted upon himself to believe in it, is liable to death. For example, if he stood before a statue and said to it: "You are my god." And even if he took a stone or a brick, stood it upright and accepted it upon himself as a deity by saying: "You are my god" – he is liable to death (Sanhedrin 60b; 63a; Rambam, ibid. 3:4).

In addition, the Torah forbade expressing honour or love toward an idol. Therefore, it is forbidden to embrace or kiss the statue, and it is forbidden to wash it, clean it, clothe it, put shoes on it, or clean the place where it is located. However, one who does one of these things is not liable to death, since he did not worship it through one of the services particular to it or through one of the four services performed in the Temple. Nor is he liable to lashes, since there is no detailed and explicit prohibition against these acts; rather, they fall under the general prohibition (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:6).

It is forbidden to make a statue in order to worship it, as it is stated (Shemot 20:4): "You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness of anything that is in the heavens above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth." Even one who does not believe in idols is forbidden to make a statue for others who intend to worship it, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols, nor make for yourselves molten gods; I am the Lord your God." Included in this prohibition, it is also forbidden for a person to buy a statue for himself. If he transgressed and made a statue or bought one, he is liable to lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:9; Rambam's Sefer Ha-mitzvot, negative commandment 3).

It is forbidden to prophesy in the name of an idol, even if the prophecy is for the sake of observing the mitzvot, for example, if he says: A certain idol revealed itself to me and commanded that you perform this mitzva which is written in the Torah. If he transgressed and prophesied in the name of an idol, he is liable to death by strangulation, as it is stated (Devarim 18:20): "And he who speaks in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die" (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 5:6).

The Torah further forbade deriving benefit from idolatry, from its service utensils, from its ornaments, and from the offerings that were brought before it as a sacrifice, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25-26): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn with fire… you shall utterly detest it and you shall utterly abhor it, for it is a banned thing (ḥerem)." And it is stated (Devarim 13:18): "And nothing of the banned thing shall cleave to your hand." This prohibition and its safeguards will be explained at length in chapter 10.

As an extension of the mitzva to detest and abhor idolatry, the Sages decreed impurity upon idolatry. That is, they decreed that the statues, their service utensils, and what was offered before them are "primary sources of impurity" (avot ha-tum'a), and if they touch a person or vessels, foods or liquids, they render them impure (Rambam, Hilkhot She'ar Avot Ha-tum'ot 6:1).

The Torah warned not to turn to idols and take an interest in them, nor to be drawn after them, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols." This prohibition and its safeguards will be explained below in chapter 13.

The Torah forbade vowing or swearing in the name of idolatry, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And make no mention of the name of other gods; let it not be heard from your mouth." Included in this prohibition is not to mention it in an honourable manner, as explained below (14:1-2).

sections.title: Idolatry in Partnership and Similar Cases
sections.html:
Included in the prohibition of idolatry, it is also forbidden to worship idolatry in partnership (shituf). That is, even when a Jew believes that the Lord, who revealed Himself to Israel, is the God of gods, if in addition he believes in an idol that has independent power of its own and can do good or harm, and he worships it as well or accepts it as well as a deity, his law is that of an idol worshipper in every respect. As it is stated (Shemot 20:3): "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Rambam, Hilkhot Yesodei Ha-Torah 1:6-7; Yere'im 243; Semag, negative commandment 1). It is likewise stated (Shemot 22:19): "He who sacrifices to the gods, except to the Lord alone, shall be utterly destroyed." Israel was also especially warned regarding belief in God's unity, as it is stated (Devarim 6:4): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one" (Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 417).

However, in truth, under the laws of Heaven, the gravity of the sin of one who worships idolatry in partnership is lighter, since he also believes in God. The Sages likewise said (Sanhedrin 63a) that in the merit of Israel's continuing to believe in God when they sinned with the Golden Calf, they were saved from annihilation.2

Even one who does not believe in an idol is forbidden to perform its rite out of love or fear, that is, out of his love for a person who asked this of him, or out of his fear of a person who threatened to punish him if he did not worship the idol. Likewise, one who does not believe in an idol is forbidden to worship it because he loves its particular form or its manner of worship, or because he feared that if he did not worship it he would have bad luck and be punished. However, if he transgressed and worshipped it, he is exempt from death, since he does not believe in the divinity of the idol (Sanhedrin 61b; Rashi; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 3:6).3

Even one who believes in God alone is forbidden by Torah law to make a statue that supposedly depicts God, as it is stated (Shemot 20:20): "You shall not make with Me gods of silver, or gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves" – "that you should not say, I will make Him a kind of likeness and bow down to it" (Mekhilta ibid.). Indeed, the Torah commanded that two cherubim in human form, made of gold, be placed on the ark-cover (kaporet) in the Holy of Holies, to express the divine revelation; however, whoever deviated from the mitzva, for example by making them of silver, or making four cherubim, transgressed the Torah prohibition of making a statue for God (Mekhilta ibid.).

sections.title: The Inciter (Mesit)
sections.html:
The Torah warned with a severe warning that a Jew must not incite his fellow to worship idolatry. And if he incited, even if in practice he did not succeed in inciting him, he is liable to death by stoning (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 5:1).

The Torah commanded not to love the inciter, not to listen to his words, not to assist him in any matter, not to have mercy on him to save him if he is found in danger, not to argue in his favour without justification, and not to keep silent rather than testify against him, so that he receives the punishment fitting for his grave sin. However, at first one must try to dissuade the inciter from his sin, just as every person is obligated to rebuke his fellow so that he does not sin. But if the inciter insisted on continuing in his way, one must treat him with full severity. As it is stated (Devarim 13:7-9): "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying: Let us go and worship other gods, which you have not known, you nor your fathers; of the gods of the peoples that are round about you, near to you or far off from you, from one end of the earth to the other end of the earth; you shall not consent to him, nor listen to him; neither shall your eye pity him, nor shall you spare, nor shall you conceal him" (Sanhedrin 61a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 5:1-4).

If the inciter tried to incite two people, they will be the witnesses to his sin. And if he tried to incite one person, although with all other sins between man and God no effort is made to incriminate a person in order to punish him, with this sin the Torah commanded to try to incriminate him. To this end, two witnesses must be hidden, and the inciter asked again to say what he said; and if, despite being asked, "How can we abandon the Lord our God and worship wood and stones?" he insisted on inciting, the hidden witnesses testify against him in the court.

In the procedures of the court too, the law of the inciter is treated stringently. For in all proceedings concerning those liable to death, if the accused was acquitted and a new claim arose against him, the case is not reopened, whereas with the inciter it is reopened. In all proceedings concerning those liable to death, care is taken to seat judges who are raising children, so that they will be merciful, whereas in the case of the inciter, old and childless men are also seated, so that they will not have mercy on him (Sanhedrin 33b; 36b; Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 11:5).

If the court found that the inciter was guilty and liable to death, the man whom he tried to incite to worship idolatry and to bring his soul down to the netherworld should be the one who begins his execution. As it is stated (ibid. 13:10-12): "But you shall surely kill him; your hand shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hand of all the people. And you shall stone him with stones, and he shall die, because he sought to draw you away from the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. And all Israel shall hear and fear, and shall do no more any such wickedness as this in your midst." All this is in order to deter from the grave sin of inciting to idolatry, which is the root of all sins.4

sections.title: The Subverted City (Ir Ha-nidaḥat)
sections.html:
When the majority of the inhabitants of a city in Israel were led astray to sin through idolatry, their law is that of rebels against the kingdom, and it is a mitzva to execute all the sinners by the sword, to put the animals to death, to burn all the city's houses and property, and to leave it a ruin forever. As it is stated (Devarim 13:13-18): "If you hear concerning one of your cities, which the Lord your God gives you to dwell there, saying: Certain base men have gone out from your midst and have led astray the inhabitants of their city, saying: Let us go and worship other gods, which you have not known; then you shall inquire, and investigate, and ask diligently, and behold, if it is true and the thing certain, that this abomination has been done in your midst, you shall surely smite the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword, destroying it utterly and all that is in it, and its cattle, with the edge of the sword. And you shall gather all its spoil into the midst of its square, and shall burn with fire the city and all its spoil entirely unto the Lord your God; and it shall be a mound forever; it shall not be built again. And nothing of the banned thing shall cleave to your hand, so that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of His anger, and show you mercy, and have compassion upon you, and multiply you, as He has sworn to your fathers."

When a person sins through idolatry not within the framework of a subverted city, he is punished with the most severe death – death by stoning; however, only he is punished, and he bequeaths his property to his heirs. In contrast, those who sin within the framework of a subverted city are punished with a lighter death – death by the sword; however, all their property is burned, and consequently they do not bequeath it to their relatives.

Before this severe sentence is carried out, the Torah instructed to inquire and investigate the matter well. If it became clear that this had occurred, the Great Court of seventy-one elders would send Torah scholars to the people of the city to warn them and bring them back in repentance. If they did not repent, the Great Court would instruct Israel to send an army against them, in order to bring them to trial before a Minor Sanhedrin of twenty-three judges. Anyone against whom two witnesses testified that, after being warned, he intentionally worshipped idolatry, is liable to death. If it became clear that the sinners were a minority of the city's inhabitants, the sinners are punished by stoning and their property goes to their heirs. And if it became clear that the majority of the city's inhabitants were liable to death, the Great Court would determine that their law is that of a subverted city, and all the sinners are killed by the sword, and their property and houses are burned. Those who did not sin are not killed, but their property is burned together with the property of the rest of the people of the city. And even if those who did not sin were righteous, their property is burned, since their wealth caused them to remain living with the wicked despite the danger of being badly influenced by them (Sanhedrin 112a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 4:6-7).

Jerusalem, and likewise the cities of refuge, do not become a subverted city, as it is stated (Devarim 13:13): "in one of your cities, which the Lord your God gives you to dwell there." Thus only an ordinary city belonging to one of the tribes of Israel can become a subverted city, but Jerusalem, which was not divided among the tribes, and likewise a city given to the Levites to serve as a city of refuge for those who kill unintentionally, cannot become a subverted city (Bava Kamma 82b; Rambam, ibid. 4:4).

A subverted city is not made on the frontier, that is, at the border of Israel, so that gentiles will not enter the Land of Israel through the ruined place.

Likewise, a second subverted city is not made in a region where one was already made, so that the land will not become "bald" (with a region without settlement). The land is divided into three regions: Yehuda, the Galil, and Transjordan (Ever Ha-yarden). In addition, even in another generation, it is not permitted to make a third subverted city, even in a region where a subverted city has not yet been made, for in all generations only two subverted cities may be made and no more (Sanhedrin 16b; Ra'avad, Yere'im, Meiri; Pri Ḥadash).5

sections.title: Laws of the Subverted City
sections.html:
A city becomes a "subverted city" only if at least two men from that city and that tribe lead the people of their city astray. But if those who led it astray came from outside it, or its people began to be persuaded to worship idolatry on their own, or women led them astray, it is not judged as a subverted city (Sanhedrin 111b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 4:2).

The law of the subverted city applies on condition that the number of the majority of the city's inhabitants who worshipped idolatry was a hundred or more, for if they were fewer, it is not a city but a village. On the other hand, if the number of sinners reached the majority of a tribe of Israel, it is no longer a city but a metropolis, and it does not have the law of a subverted city (Sanhedrin 15b; Rambam, ibid.).

A caravan that passed through a subverted city, if it encamped in the city for thirty days, has the law of the people of the city, and they are counted with the people of the city for the purpose of determining the majority. If they encamped there for less than thirty days, their law is that of private individuals, each of whom is judged alone for his sin (Rambam, ibid. 4:9).

The property of the people of the city must be burned, and it is forbidden to derive benefit from it, and one who transgresses and derives benefit is liable to lashes. The property that must be burned is the property of the people of the city that is located in the city, but the property of people outside the city that was deposited with the people of the city is not burned. Property of the people of the city that was outside the city is also not burned: if it belongs to people who did not sin, it remains in their possession, and if it belongs to wicked people who were killed, the property is given to their heirs (ibid. 4:7, 10).

The city's animals are also killed, and if there were animals that had been consecrated as sacrifices, they are not offered, for "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" (Mishlei 21:27). However, since they were consecrated, they are not killed directly; rather, they are caused to die on their own. Sacred writings belonging to the people of the city are to be put away in storage (geniza), for it is forbidden to burn them, yet on the other hand it is forbidden to derive benefit from them (ibid. 11-15).

It is forbidden to build houses on the ruins of a subverted city, but it is permitted to grow fruit trees (ibid. 4:8).

The Sages disagreed on the question of whether the law of the subverted city was meant to teach practical halakha or to teach a principle. Some say there was a case in which a subverted city was judged, as Rabbi Yonatan said: "I saw it, and I sat on its mound." And many say: "There never was a subverted city and there never will be. Why then was it written? Expound it and receive reward" (Sanhedrin 71a; 113a). That is, by studying the law of the subverted city we will understand the severity of idolatry and distance ourselves from any trace of it, and this will be our reward. The reason it cannot happen is that it is hard to suppose that valid witnesses will be found who will testify about the majority of the people of the city that they worshipped idolatry despite having been warned. Furthermore, Rabbi Eliezer said that even if there was a single mezuza in the city, it is not made a subverted city, and it is hard to suppose that not even one person there would be found who had affixed a mezuza in his house.

Although the law of the subverted city is severe and cruel, the Sages learned from the Torah that in truth there is mercy in it, for it prevents society from deteriorating into idolatry, which leads to acts many times more cruel. This is what the Sages said in the Mishna (Sanhedrin 111b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: If you carry out judgment on the subverted city, I account it to you as if you were offering a whole burnt offering before Me," as it is stated: "entirely unto the Lord your God." "For as long as the wicked are in the world, there is fierce anger in the world; when the wicked perish from the world, fierce anger departs from the world." Even according to the view that in practice there never was a subverted city, there is mercy in this law, because the inner consensus that it is fitting to carry out harsh judgment upon a group that bands together to worship idolatry prevents calamity and arouses mercy.

sections.title: The Blasphemer (Megadef)
sections.html:
A curse is speech that expresses a strong desire that something bad should happen to the one cursed. The Torah forbade cursing a Jew, and anyone who curses a Jew is liable to lashes, provided that he curses with the name of God or with one of His appellations, in Hebrew or in another language, for example, if he said: "In the name of the Merciful and Gracious One, may So-and-so's name be blotted out" (Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 26:1-4). And there is a more severe curse, in which the one cursing uses the name of God in order to disgrace the honour of Heaven and to curse God, for example, if he says "E-l-o-h-i-m" should curse "A-d-o-n-a-i," and its punishment is death. As it is stated (Vayikra 24:16): "And he who blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death; all the congregation shall surely stone him; the stranger as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death." One who sins with this severe curse, whose punishment is death, is called a "megadef" (blasphemer), and the Sages referred to the sin of the one who curses by a euphemism (literally, "abundance of light") as "blessing the Name."

This prohibition also involves idolatry, for the blasphemer relates to God the way idol worshippers relate to their idols: when they thought that one of the idols was threatening them, they sometimes sought help from another idol against it, and in its name they cursed the idol they thought was threatening them. Similarly, the blasphemer holds that God appears in different powers, and he tries to enlist the help of one power against the other. And even if he curses with the same name, for example, if he says: "May A-d-o-n-a-i curse A-d-o-n-a-i," this is like one who holds that the same idol has two manifestations and two statues, one in his favour and the other to his detriment.6

Just as one who worships idolatry is liable to death by stoning, so the blasphemer is liable to death by stoning. In addition, because of the severity of their sin, unlike all others liable to death, both of them are hanged after their stoning.

One who hears a curse from a gentile is not obligated to tear his garment, but one who hears a Jew desecrating God's name and cursing His name must tear his garments (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 2:10). And so it is related in the Prophets (II Melakhim 18:28-37) about Ravshakeh, who was an apostate Jew who joined the Assyrian camp, and when the Assyrian army besieged Jerusalem he proposed to Israel that they surrender and go into exile, and in the course of this he cursed the name of the God of Israel, and for this those who heard tore their garments.

One incident of a blasphemer is related in the Torah, as it is stated (Vayikra 24:10-23): "And the son of an Israelite woman, whose father was an Egyptian man, went out among the children of Israel; and the son of the Israelite woman and a man of Israel strove together in the camp. And the son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name and cursed; and they brought him to Moshe. And his mother's name was Shelomit, the daughter of Divri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him in custody, that it might be declared to them according to the word of the Lord. And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying: Bring forth the one who cursed outside the camp, and let all who heard him lay their hands upon his head, and let all the congregation stone him. And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin. And he who blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death; all the congregation shall surely stone him; the stranger as well as the native-born, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death." From this the Torah went on to warn the children of Israel not to harm one another or one another's property, as it is stated: "And he who smites any human being shall surely be put to death… And if a man maims his fellow, as he has done, so shall it be done to him… And he who smites an animal shall pay for it… You shall have one law, for the stranger as well as for the native-born, for I am the Lord your God." This teaches us that precisely through strengthening the honour of Heaven, one can strengthen the protection of the life of man, who was created in the image of God. And conversely, when people are not careful about the honour of Heaven, they subsequently come to grievous harm to man.

sections.title: The Mitzva to Destroy Idolatry from the Land and from Jewish Possession
sections.html:
The destiny of Israel is to establish in the Land of Israel a kingdom that walks in the ways of God, does righteousness and justice, and merits God's blessing, and through this reveals to the whole world God's light and His blessing. However, this great vision will be destroyed if they abandon the way of God to worship idols. As it is stated in the passage "Ve-haya im shamo'a" (Devarim 11:16-17): "Take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow down to them; and the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and He shut up the heavens so that there be no rain, and the ground not yield its produce, and you perish quickly from off the good land which the Lord gives you" (and likewise ibid. 8:12-14, 17, 19; 6:10-12, 14; 32:15-16, and elsewhere).

In order to prevent us from being drawn after idolatry, and in order to express the proper attitude toward its falsehood and wickedness, it is a mitzva to destroy the statues of the idols, the asherah trees, their altars and their cultic utensils. As it is stated (Shemot 34:13): "For you shall tear down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their asherim." And it is stated (Devarim 12:2-3): "You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations that you are dispossessing served their gods, upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every leafy tree. And you shall tear down their altars, and break their pillars, and burn their asherim with fire; and you shall hew down the graven images of their gods, and you shall destroy their name out of that place." And it is stated (ibid. 7:1-6): "When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are going to possess, and casts out many nations before you… But thus shall you deal with them: you shall tear down their altars, and break their pillars, and hew down their asherim, and burn their graven images with fire." There are two parts to the mitzva to destroy idolatry: 1) For the Jewish people as a whole in the Land, to destroy idolatry from the Land of Israel. 2) For each and every individual Jew throughout the world, to destroy idolatry from his possession (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:1; Ramban, Kiddushin 37a; Gra 146:20).

1) The Jewish people as a whole are commanded to destroy idolatry from the Land of Israel. The Sages learned from the verses of the Torah that the destruction of idolatry at the time of the conquest of the Land is carried out in two stages. First, in the course of the conquest, the asherah trees must be cut down and the statues and altars broken, and the war continued until its end. Afterward, one must go back and uproot the asherim and burn them, and likewise destroy the statues and the pillars. As it is stated (Devarim 12:2): "You shall surely destroy (abed te'abdun) – destroy, and afterward you shall destroy" (Avoda Zara 45b).

2) Every Jew is commanded to destroy from the world any idolatry that has come into his share, whether he is in the Land or outside the Land. That is, in addition to the prohibition of deriving benefit from idolatry (which will be studied below in chapter 10), every Jew is commanded to destroy idolatry that has come into his possession, so that no person will ever derive benefit from it. Therefore, a Jew who bought property that included idolatry, or inherited idolatry, or found it and took it, since it has come into his share – he is obligated to destroy it. But as long as the idolatry has not come into his possession, the individual has no mitzva to destroy it.7

sections.title: Idol Worshippers Living in the Land
sections.html:
It is a mitzva not to allow idol worshippers to live in the Land, as it is stated (Shemot 23:32-33): "You shall make no covenant with them, nor with their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against Me; for you will serve their gods, for it will be a snare to you." It is likewise stated (Devarim 7:2-4): "You shall make no covenant with them, nor show favour to them (lo teḥonem). Neither shall you intermarry with them… For he will turn away your son from following Me, and they will serve other gods" (see Peninei Halakha, Ha-am Ve-ha'aretz 5:1). However, in practice, throughout all the years of the Jewish people's existence in its Land, idol worshippers also lived in the Land. The Torah too refers to this, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:47): "And if a stranger or sojourner with you becomes rich, and your brother becomes poor beside him, and sells himself to the stranger or sojourner with you, or to an offshoot of a stranger's family (eker mishpaḥat ger)." "An offshoot of a stranger's family" is an idol worshipper (Rashi and Ramban ibid.; Arakhin 30b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avadim 1:3). Thus we find in the Torah a situation in which gentiles keep idolatry in the Land in their private possession, and a Jew sold himself to them as a slave, and the Torah commanded to redeem him, but did not command to harm the gentile and his idolatry. One must ask: how is it possible that he has idolatry in his possession, after we were commanded to eradicate idolatry from the Land?

There are three possible explanations. The first: when we have the upper hand to fulfil the mitzva, we are obligated not to leave idol worshippers in the Land; however, already in the Torah it is stated that we will reach this gradually, as it is stated (Shemot 23:30): "Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and inherit the land." It turns out that the Torah's mitzva to redeem one who was sold to an idol worshipper in the Land refers to the interim period in which we do not yet have the upper hand to expel all the idol worshippers from the Land (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 10:6).

The second: the prohibition of leaving idol worshippers in the Land refers to the seven Canaanite nations only, as it is stated (Devarim 7:1-2): "When the Lord your God brings you into the land… and casts out many nations before you… seven nations… and you shall smite them; you shall utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, nor show favour to them" (Rashi, Gittin 45a; Ra'avad, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 10:6; Semag, negative commandments 47; Tosafot, Yevamot 23a, s.v. "Hahu," in the third explanation).

The third: the obligation to expel the idol worshippers and to eradicate their idols applies at the time of the conquest of the Land, as long as the war continues. But one who remains in the Land after the war, as long as he accepts the sovereignty of Israel, is not expelled from the Land. And if he associates the name of Heaven with his idolatry, he need not, even from the outset, eradicate idolatry from his home, for according to most halakhic authorities Noahides are not prohibited from idolatry in partnership.8

At the time of the establishment of the State of Israel the question arose whether, according to halakha, it is permitted to allow members of the Muslim and Christian religions to live in the Land with equal rights, as is customary in democratic countries. Rav Yitzḥak Herzog ztz"l, the great Torah scholar who served as Chief Rabbi at the time of the establishment of the State of Israel, dealt with this question at length, and wrote that even if they were outright idol worshippers, who according to many may not live in the Land, it would be permitted. This is because the nations of the world gave their consent to the establishment of the state on condition "that there shall be no discrimination of any kind in the state on the basis of race, religion, language or sex" (UN resolution). There is no doubt that without this consent the State of Israel could not have been established, and even after its establishment, until our righteous Mashiaḥ comes, it is impossible for it to survive, surrounded by enemies, without this consent. In such a situation, Rav Herzog wrote: "There will not be found a rabbi in Israel with a brain and sound judgment" who would hold that we must give up the establishment of the State of Israel, through which we fulfil the mitzva of settling the Land and save many Jewish lives. Moreover, the entire aim of the prohibition against their dwelling in our Land is that they should not influence us, and through the establishment of the state, Jewish identity will be strengthened, and consequently their influence on us will diminish.

He further added that the Christians associate the name of Heaven in their worship, and the main halakhic ruling follows those who hold that Noahides are not prohibited from worshipping idolatry in partnership, and therefore it is permitted to leave them in the Land.9

sections.title: Caution Regarding Idol Worshippers
sections.html:
Since idol worshippers behaved with wickedness and corruption, and were suspected of murder, the Sages enacted ordinances intended to protect Israel from them. Among these, the Sages ruled that a Jew is forbidden to be alone with them in a secluded place, lest they murder him (Avoda Zara 22a; SA YD 153:2). They likewise forbade giving a Jewish child to a wet nurse who worships idolatry, lest she murder him. Only inside a Jewish home, when other people are present there, did they permit hiring her to nurse him (Avoda Zara 26a; SA YD 154:1).

The Sages further forbade having one's hair cut by an idol worshipper, lest he use the haircutting knife to murder the Jew, but in a place where people pass by and see, it is permitted (Avoda Zara 27a; SA YD 156:1). They likewise forbade receiving medical treatment from an idol worshipper, lest he murder the patient. Even in a situation where, without treatment, the patient will most likely die, he should not be treated by him. However, if he is an expert physician, there is no concern that he will murder him, for if the patient dies his standing as a physician will be harmed and he will lose his livelihood (Avoda Zara 27a; SA YD 155:1).

The Sages likewise forbade saving an idol worshipper from death, since he is a wicked person who is liable to murder. Therefore, if he fell into a pit or the like, one should not bring him up (Avoda Zara 26a; SA YD 158:1). Likewise, if he was ill, one should not heal him (SA YD 158:1). Likewise, one does not assist an idol-worshipping woman to give birth, for one should not assist in the birth of a child who will be raised to idolatry. For this reason also one should not nurse him, for one should not assist in raising a child to idolatry (Avoda Zara 26a; SA YD 154:1-2).

However, as long as there is no war between us and them, one must avoid increasing enmity, and therefore if the Jew is a physician, a midwife or a wet nurse, which is their occupation, as long as they are paid, they should fulfil their role. For if they refuse to heal, deliver or nurse for payment, they will increase enmity. And if even refusing to heal for free will increase enmity, it is permitted to heal them even for free (Avoda Zara 26a; SA YD 154:2; 158:1, and Rema there).

Since idol worshippers were also suspected of all kinds of forbidden sexual relations, the Sages forbade sending a child to learn a trade from an idol worshipper, lest he rape him. Likewise, a woman is forbidden to be alone with idol worshippers, even when their wives are with them, lest they rape her (Avoda Zara 22a). They even forbade leaving an animal in their inn or giving them sheep to graze, lest they sin with them through the prohibition of bestiality (Avoda Zara 22a; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 22:4-5).

By God's kindness, through the blessed influence of the Torah, many nations rose from outright idolatry to idolatry with the association of the name of Heaven, which according to most halakhic authorities is not forbidden to Noahides (below, 5:8-12). In parallel, the refinement of faith also led to moral progress. And since these rabbinic prohibitions were intended to protect Israel from the dangers posed by idol worshippers, they depend on reality, and in a place where there is no concern that the gentiles will murder or rape, because these acts have become unacceptable in their eyes and they even punish them, there is no need for concern. Therefore, already some seven hundred years ago, several Rishonim wrote that in their place there was no concern about bestiality, and therefore it is permitted to give animals to the gentiles there to graze and to be alone with them (Rashba, cited in the Maggid Mishneh, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a 22:5; Ran on the Rif, Avoda Zara 7a; Meiri, Avoda Zara 15b; SA YD 153:1).

Likewise, in a place where the gentiles have become restrained from murder, and even denounce and punish murderers, so that the concern that they will murder has become remote, there is no prohibition against being alone with them on the road, or receiving medical treatment from them, or giving a child to a wet nurse to nurse him (Meiri, Avoda Zara 15b; Binat Adam, Sha'ar Beit Ha-nashim 16:26; Ḥayei Adam 11:42; MB 20:7). Likewise, when they are restrained by morality, one must save them (Meiri, Rav Kook). However, regarding gentiles who are not restrained by morality and there is a concern that they will murder, one must be careful about the prohibitions.10

sections.title: The Status of a Jew Who Worships Idolatry – the Meshumad
sections.html:
A Jew who worshipped idolatry is considered one who betrayed the people of Israel and its God, and he is called a "meshumad" (apostate), for he chose to destroy (le-hashmid) his Jewish identity. The Torah commanded not to accept a sacrifice from the meshumad, as it is stated (Vayikra 1:2): "When any man of you brings an offering to the Lord" – the Sages expounded: "'Of you' – excluding the meshumad" (Ḥullin 5a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aseh Ha-korbanot 3:3-4). In this his status is worse than that of a gentile who worships idolatry, for from the gentile a sacrifice is accepted (below, 5:3), whereas from a Jewish meshumad a sacrifice is not accepted.

In addition, since he removed himself from the community, the Torah commanded that he not eat of the Pesaḥ sacrifice, which is the sacrifice that expresses the special character (segula) of Israel. As it is stated (Shemot 12:43): "This is the statute of the Pesaḥ: no foreigner (ben nekhar) shall eat of it" – the Sages expounded: a ben nekhar is "a Jewish meshumad who worshipped idolatry" (Mekhilta).

Following on from this, the Sages enacted that a Jew who worshipped idolatry is to be regarded as a gentile. Therefore, if he slaughtered an animal, even though he slaughtered it according to the rules of halakha, his slaughter is invalid like the slaughter of a gentile (Ḥullin 5a; Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 18:4). Likewise, the mitzva to perform kindness to every Jew, including transgressors, does not apply to a meshumad.

However, in truth the meshumad is a Jew, and therefore, even though the Sages penalized him by regarding him as a gentile – and a gentile who betrothed a Jewish woman, his betrothal is void – if a Jewish meshumad betrothed a Jewish woman, she is betrothed, and likewise a Jewish woman who is a meshumad and was betrothed to a Jew is betrothed, and if they wish to separate they will require a valid get (Rambam, Hilkhot Ishut 4:15).11

sections.title: The Repentance of an Apostate to Idolatry
sections.html:
Great is repentance, which is effective for all the transgressions in the Torah, and one who repents is considered as if newly born without the transgressions he had committed. Repentance does not serve to exempt a person from punishments imposed by the court, but it is effective for the judgment of Heaven, to change the person's inner status from the state of a sinner who is far from God to the state of a ba'al teshuva (penitent) who is desired and beloved by God. The graver the sins for which one repents, the deeper and more shaking the repentance must be, so that it will be clear that the penitent has truly regretted his sins and has accepted upon himself to begin conducting himself as an upright Jew.

Therefore, ever since the period of the Geonim, it has been customary to give lashes to apostates who returned to Judaism, so that through this they would merit atonement, and thereby be able to repent truly (Rav Amram Gaon; Tur in the name of a Gaon; Rashba; SA YD 267:8). After the terrible decrees against Spanish Jewry, which lasted more than a hundred years, and in whose wake hundreds of thousands of Jews converted under threats of murder and expulsion, there were Jews who succeeded in fleeing from Spain and sought to return to their Judaism. To help them return to Israel, Rabbi Ya'akov Beirav and Rabbi Yosef Karo, together with many other Sages of Tzfat, wished to renew the semikha (ordination) with which the Sages of the Sanhedrin had been ordained since the time of Moshe Rabbeinu, which had lapsed when the Land was destroyed. This was so that the atonement of the returning anusim (forced converts) would be complete, since the lashes they would receive would carry the authority of an ordained court and would serve to exempt them from the punishments of karet. However, Rabbi Levi ben Ḥaviv, rabbi of the community in Jerusalem, opposed the renewal of semikha, and among other things argued that there was no need for ordained judges in order to give lashes to those returning to Judaism; rather, it is enough to give them lashes through an ordinary court (Responsa Maharalbaḥ, Kuntres Ha-semikha). And some say that returning apostates may give money to charity in place of the lashes, for great is charity, which saves from death. And since the rabbis did not want to make the repentance of apostates burdensome, as the years passed this ruling became more accepted.

Many instructed an apostate who returned to Judaism to immerse in a mikveh, because in his return to Israel he is similar to a convert who is born anew, and therefore he must immerse in order to re-enter Israel. In contrast, some say that only a convert must immerse in order to enter Israel, but a Jew, "even though he has sinned, he is a Jew" (Sanhedrin 44a), and therefore he does not need to immerse.

Likewise, some say that an apostate who returned to Judaism must renew the covenant with God and with Israel, and to that end he must again accept the Torah and the mitzvot before a court. This acceptance is called "kabbalat divrei ḥaverut" (accepting the obligations of fellowship), so that from then on he can be relied upon as an upright Jew. In contrast, some say that only a convert must accept upon himself Torah and mitzvot before a court, but a Jewish transgressor always remains obligated in the mitzvot; therefore he must repent, but there is no need for him to accept the Torah and the mitzvot anew.12
